kurals.tamil:
பொருளல் லவரைப் பொருளாகச் செய்யும்
பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Porulal lavaraip porulaakach cheyyum
porulalladhu illai porul.
kurals.meaning: Nothing but wealth can turn people who count for nothing into people who count for something; there is no other thing like it.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a boy nobody picks for the team. One day he brings a brand-new football, and suddenly everyone wants to play with him. He is the same boy, but now people notice him. Valluvar says money works like that ball: it makes people who were ignored get noticed.
kurals.university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of koozh (கூழ், treasury or wealth), one of the six limbs of the state named in kural 381, and it begins with a deliberately startling claim. The couplet plays on three senses of porul: ‘thing of account’, ‘worth’, and ‘wealth’, so that porulallavar are ‘those who are no-thing’, and the second line says there is no porul (thing) except porul (wealth). Parimelazhagar treats the verse as a plain statement of how the world behaves rather than a moral endorsement, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar likewise read it as a description of social esteem, not of true merit. The ytamizh text divides பொருளல்லது இல்லை, while the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh reads பொருளல்ல தில்லை; the words are the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that has wealth has friends. He that has wealth has kinsmen. He that has wealth is regarded as a true man in the world. He that has wealth is regarded as a learned man.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna urges the grieving Yudhishthira not to renounce the kingdom, arguing that wealth is what makes a person count in the eyes of the world.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna and Valluvar make the same observation: wealth makes a person be seen as someone of worth.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section VIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close match; Arjuna’s speech is a rhetorical plea in a debate, while the Kural states it as a maxim.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The poor is hated even of his own neighbour: but the rich hath many friends.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb observes that the poor are shunned even by those nearest them, while the rich attract a crowd of friends.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes how wealth turns an ignored person into a sought-after one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on social esteem; the proverb stresses friendship rather than worth.

islam.quote_or_event: “And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient.”
islam.explanation: God reminds the Prophet that he once lacked means and that God raised him to sufficiency, as one of several favours listed in the sura.
islam.tie_back: The verse shares the Kural’s picture of someone raised from nothing by provision, but it credits God rather than wealth itself.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial match: the verse is about divine favour and sufficiency, not social esteem conferred by money.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They make a banquet for revelry; wine makes life merry, and money answers every need.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet notes, with his usual dry realism, that money is what meets every demand of life.
judaism.tie_back: Kohelet and the Kural share the same unsentimental claim that wealth is the one thing that answers for everything else.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 10:19 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on wealth’s all-sufficiency; Kohelet does not speak specifically of raising the lowly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The second thing, having got wealth by legitimate means, is the wish: ‘May fame come to me, together with my family and mentors.’”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that the second hard-won desire of a householder is fame, which follows once wealth has been legitimately gained.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta, like the Kural, sees standing and reputation as things that come after wealth.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.61, Pattakamma Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Moderate match: the sutta lists fame after wealth as a wish, not as a claim that wealth confers worth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But if you work, the idle will soon envy you as you grow rich, for fame and renown attend on wealth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother Perses that honest work leads to riches, and that riches bring fame and renown with them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod gives the same reason as Valluvar: esteem goes wherever wealth goes.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match; Hesiod ties the renown to wealth earned by work, as the chapter as a whole does.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Adam Smith describes how people are naturally disposed to admire and almost worship the rich and great while neglecting persons of poor and mean condition, and he calls this disposition the great cause of the corruption of our moral sentiments.
philosophy.explanation: Smith explains that we tend to honour the wealthy because we sympathise more easily with their good fortune, even when they do not deserve it.
philosophy.tie_back: Smith explains why the Kural’s observation holds, while warning that the esteem wealth brings is not moral worth.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I, Section III, Chapter 3
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a well-known chapter, not checked verbatim; strong thematic fit.

kurals.tamil:
இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர் செல்வரை
எல்லாரும் செய்வர் சிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Illaarai ellaarum elluvar selvarai
ellaarum seyvar sirappu.
kurals.meaning: Everyone looks down on those who have nothing, and everyone honours those who are rich.
kurals.elementary: Two children come to a party. One wears a torn shirt and the other a shiny new outfit. Some people smile at the second child and ignore the first, even though nothing else is different. Valluvar is telling us this happens, so that we notice it and do not treat people unfairly.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a tight parallelism: illaarai (the have-nots) against selvarai (the wealthy), and ellaarum elluvar (all scorn) against ellaarum seyvar sirappu (all do honour). Mu. Varadarasanar adds in parentheses that the poor are scorned even if they have other virtues and the rich honoured even if they have none, which makes the verse a comment on injustice as well as a fact of life. Parimelazhagar reads it, like 751, as a reason for the ruler to gather wealth: a king without a treasury would suffer the same contempt. Kalaignar’s gloss calls this simply the way of the world (உலக நடப்பு). The sandhi-joined text reads இல்லாரை யெல்லாரு மெள்ளுவர், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is seen that a poor man, even when he stands near, is accused falsely. Poverty is a state of sinfulness. It behoveth thee not to applaud poverty, therefore.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna argues that society treats the poor with suspicion and contempt, so poverty should not be praised.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna sees the same contempt for the poor that Valluvar describes.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section VIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on scorn of the poor; Arjuna goes further than the Kural in calling poverty sinful.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool.”
christianity.explanation: James rebukes a congregation that gives the best seat to a rich visitor and pushes a poor one to the floor.
christianity.tie_back: James shows the very scene the Kural describes, honour for the rich and scorn for the poor, and calls it sinful partiality.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one description of the behaviour; James condemns it where the Kural only observes it.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one’s] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an grants that wealth adorns worldly life but says lasting good deeds count for more with God.
islam.tie_back: The verse agrees that wealth brings worldly honour, as the Kural says, while pointing to a truer measure of worth.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial match: it speaks of wealth as worldly adornment, not directly of how people treat rich and poor.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So I observed: Wisdom is better than valor; but The wisdom of the poor is scorned, And their words are not heeded.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet tells of a poor wise man who saved a city yet was forgotten, and concludes that the poor person’s wisdom is despised.
judaism.tie_back: Kohelet sees the same scorn for the poor as the Kural, even when the poor have real merit.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 9:16 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match, and it echoes Mu. Varadarasanar’s reading that the poor are scorned whatever their virtues.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada calls contentment the greatest wealth, measuring worth by inner qualities rather than possessions.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching places real value in contentment and virtue, not in what a person owns.
buddhism.tie_back: This is a counterweight to the Kural’s observation: the world honours the rich, but the Dhamma honours the content.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Contrast rather than parallel, recalled from memory; no Buddhist text found stating the Kural’s observation directly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “An evil shame is the needy man’s companion, shame which both greatly harms and prospers men: shame is with poverty, but confidence with wealth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says that poverty brings shame with it and wealth brings confidence and standing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s shame of poverty and confidence of wealth mirror the Kural’s scorn and honour.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match; Hesiod speaks of the person’s own shame, the Kural of others’ contempt.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Juvenal’s third satire complains that the hardest thing about unhappy poverty is that it makes people ridiculous, and it describes the poor man in Rome mocked for his torn cloak and patched shoes.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman satirist protests that in Rome the poor are laughed at and shut out while the rich are courted.
philosophy.tie_back: Juvenal gives the angry version of the Kural’s calm observation that all scorn the poor.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line, not checked against a live translation; Juvenal is a satirist rather than a philosopher.

kurals.tamil:
பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம் இருளறுக்கும்
எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Porulennum poyyaa vilakkam irularukkum
enniya theyaththuch chendru.
kurals.meaning: Wealth is a lamp that never fails: carried into any land its owner chooses, it cuts through the darkness there, above all the darkness of hostility.
kurals.elementary: Think of a torch that never runs out of batteries. Wherever you walk at night, it lights the path. Valluvar says money can be like that: when you go to a new place, it can help you make friends and solve problems.
kurals.university: The metaphor pairs poyyaa vilakkam (the lamp that does not fail or lie) with iruL (darkness), and the second line sends the lamp to enniya theyam, ‘the country one has in mind’ (theyam from Sanskrit desha). Parimelazhagar glosses the darkness as enmity (பகையாகிய இருள்), and Pope and Drew’s English follows him with ‘the darkness (of enmity)’; Solomon Pappaiah likewise says wealth enters even foreign lands and dispels the darkness of hostility. Mu. Varadarasanar reads iruL more broadly as any obstacle (இடையூறு), and Kalaignar as suffering (துன்பம்). The verse sets up 759, where wealth becomes the sharpest weapon against a foe’s pride. The sandhi-joined text reads விளக்க மிருளறுக்கு மெண்ணிய, which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra lists dana, giving gifts, among the four means (upayas) a ruler uses with other states, alongside conciliation, sowing dissension and force, so that gifts can turn a hostile neighbour into an ally.
hinduism.explanation: Indian statecraft treated well-placed gifts of wealth as a standard way to win over enemies without war.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s lamp at work: wealth sent into another land to dispel the darkness of enmity.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra (four upayas: sama, dana, bheda, danda), trans. R. Shamasastry
hinduism._accuracy_note: Well-established doctrine, summarised without a specific verified passage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I say unto you, Make unto yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into the everlasting habitations.”
christianity.explanation: After the parable of the shrewd steward, Jesus tells his disciples to use worldly wealth to make friends who will welcome them later.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus, like Valluvar, sees wealth as something that turns strangers into friends.
christianity.source: Luke 16:9 (KJV), as quoted in John Wesley, Sermon 50
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified as quoted in Wesley’s sermon; the fit is partial, since Luke points to eternal welcome rather than dispelling enmity.

islam.quote_or_event: “Zakah expenditures are only for the poor and for the needy and for those employed to collect [zakah] and for bringing hearts together [for Islam] and for freeing captives [or slaves] and for those in debt and for the cause of Allah and for the [stranded] traveler.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an sets aside a share of zakat for ‘bringing hearts together’, meaning people whose hostility could be softened and whose goodwill could be won by wealth.
islam.tie_back: This category of zakat recipients is a direct religious use of wealth to dispel enmity, as the Kural describes.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on wealth softening hostility; the verse lists eight categories, and only one is relevant here.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A gift in secret subdues anger, A present in private, fierce rage.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that a well-timed private gift calms even fierce anger.
judaism.tie_back: The proverb and the Kural agree that wealth can put out the darkness of hostility.
judaism.source: Proverbs 21:14 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on wealth dissolving enmity; Proverbs speaks of individuals, the Kural of lands.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he defends himself against threats from such things as fire, flood, rulers, bandits, or unloved heirs. He keeps himself safe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists protecting oneself against dangers as the second fitting use of rightly earned wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lamp, rightly earned wealth here drives off threats wherever they arise.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.61, Pattakamma Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on wealth as protection; the sutta does not use the image of light or foreign lands.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the myth of Danaë, her father Acrisius locks her in a bronze chamber, but Zeus reaches her as a shower of gold that passes through the roof; Roman moralists such as Horace later read the story as showing that gold gets through every barrier.
greek_mythology.explanation: Gold enters the one place that was sealed against every visitor.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lamp, gold goes wherever it is aimed and gets past whatever stands in the way.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The myth itself is about divine union; reading it as the power of gold is a later Roman moral gloss.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero, writing to Atticus, recalls Philip of Macedon’s saying that any fortress could be taken if only a donkey laden with gold could climb up to it.
philosophy.explanation: Philip’s point was that gold opens gates that armies cannot.
philosophy.tie_back: Philip’s donkey of gold is the Kural’s lamp carried into an enemy’s land to undo its resistance.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus 1.16.12; also Plutarch, Sayings of Kings
philosophy._accuracy_note: Well-known anecdote summarised from memory; Philip used gold to bribe rather than to reconcile, which is a darker sense than the Kural’s.

kurals.tamil:
அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும் திறனறிந்து
தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aran eenum inbamum eenum thiranarindhu
theedhindri vandha porul.
kurals.meaning: Wealth gained by knowing the right ways and without doing wrong gives birth to both virtue and happiness.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two children selling lemonade. One makes it carefully and charges a fair price. The other sneaks sugar from a neighbour and cheats customers. Only the first can enjoy the money without worry and use it to do kind things. Valluvar says honest money brings both goodness and happiness.
kurals.university: The verb eenum (ஈனும், ‘brings forth, gives birth to’) is repeated for both aram (virtue) and inbam (pleasure or happiness), so wealth is pictured as the parent of the other two purusharthas. The conditions are thiran arindhu, ‘knowing the proper means’, and theedhu indri, ‘without evil’. Parimelazhagar takes the proper means to be those fitting one’s station and the law, and the absence of evil to mean acquiring without harm or deceit to others. Sivayogi Sivakumar adds that it means seeking wealth with knowledge of one’s own ability and harming no one. The sandhi-joined text reads அறனீனு மின்பமு மீனுந், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti opens its rules for the householder by telling him to gain his living by a blameless occupation that causes little or no pain to others, and to gather wealth only enough for his proper needs.
hinduism.explanation: The dharma texts treat earning as a duty that must be carried out without harming other beings.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s theedhindri vandha porul, wealth that comes without harm, as the basis of a righteous household.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of well-known verses; Manu adds limits on accumulation that the Kural does not stress.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the former thief to earn honestly so that he can be generous to people in need.
christianity.tie_back: Paul, like Valluvar, links honestly earned wealth to the ability to do good.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on honest gain producing virtue; Paul does not mention pleasure.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, spend from the good things which you have earned and from that which We have produced for you from the earth.”
islam.explanation: Believers are told to give in charity from the good and lawful things they have earned.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an and the Kural agree that lawfully earned wealth is what virtue is built on.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on virtue flowing from good earnings; enjoyment is not the verse’s focus.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You shall enjoy the fruit of your labors; you shall be happy and you shall prosper.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm promises that someone who walks in God’s ways will enjoy what their own hands have earned.
judaism.tie_back: Honest labour producing happiness is the inbam half of the Kural’s promise.
judaism.source: Psalm 128:2 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on the happiness of righteous earnings; the virtue side is implied by the psalm’s context.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what is the happiness of ownership? It’s when a gentleman owns legitimate wealth that he has earned by his own efforts and initiative, built up with his own hands, gathered by the sweat of the brow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that a layperson finds real happiness in owning wealth that was legitimately earned, and further happiness in using it to make merit.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta’s legitimate wealth that brings both happiness and merit is the Kural’s wealth that yields both inbam and aram.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, including the pairing of happiness with merit-making.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Through work men grow rich in flocks and substance, and working they are much better loved by the immortals.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches that honest work brings wealth and also the favour of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: For Hesiod as for Valluvar, rightly gained wealth brings prosperity and divine favour together.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match; ‘loved by the immortals’ stands in for virtue rather than naming it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In On the Happy Life, Seneca argues that a philosopher may own ample wealth provided it was taken from no one, is not stained with another’s blood, and was gained without wronging anyone.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca answers critics of his riches by saying wealth is no disgrace to a wise man if it was honestly acquired and used well.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca’s conditions match the Kural’s theedhindri, wealth that comes without evil.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of well-known chapters, not checked verbatim.

kurals.tamil:
அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம்
புல்லார் புரள விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arulodum anbodum vaaraap porulaakkam
pullaar purala vidal.
kurals.meaning: Wealth that does not come together with compassion and love should not be embraced; let it roll away.
kurals.elementary: Suppose you could win a big prize, but only by being mean to a friend. Valluvar says to let that prize go. Money that makes you unkind is like a shiny apple that is rotten inside.
kurals.university: The first line names two qualities the earning must carry: arul (அருள், compassion toward all beings, the subject of chapter 25) and anbu (அன்பு, affection toward one’s own, the subject of chapter 8). The second line is vivid: pullaar, ‘not embracing’ (from pullu, to hug or cling), and purala vidal, ‘letting it roll off’, as one lets go of something that slips from the arms. Parimelazhagar applies the verse to the ruler, who should refuse revenue gathered by cruelty to his subjects, and Pope and Drew’s English accordingly begins with ‘(Kings) should rather avoid’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah generalise it to anyone who earns. The sandhi-joined text reads அருளொடு மன்பொடும், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The first verse of the Isha Upanishad teaches that all this is pervaded by the Lord, that one should enjoy by renunciation, and that one should not covet anyone’s wealth (ma gridhah kasya svid dhanam).
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that wealth is to be enjoyed with detachment and never grasped from others.
hinduism.tie_back: The Upanishad’s refusal to grasp at others’ wealth matches the Kural’s advice to let wrongly gained wealth roll away.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Thematic match on not grasping wealth; the Upanishad’s frame is spiritual detachment, not compassion in earning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We are. Thirdly, to gain all we can without hurting our neighbour. But this we may not, cannot do, if we love our neighbour as ourselves.”
christianity.explanation: Wesley tells Methodists to gain all they can, but never by harming a neighbour’s body, soul or livelihood, since that breaks the law of love.
christianity.tie_back: Wesley’s rule that gain must never break love for one’s neighbour is the Kural’s rule that gain must come with anbu and arul.
christianity.source: John Wesley, Sermon 50, The Use of Money, I.3
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on refusing gain that breaks love; the odd punctuation is in the source.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly but only [in lawful] business by mutual consent.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids taking others’ wealth unjustly and allows only fair trade that both sides agree to.
islam.tie_back: Both texts reject wealth that comes at the cost of justice and goodwill toward others.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on refusing unjust gain; the Qur’an frames it as justice, the Kural as compassion and love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ill-gotten wealth is of no avail, But righteousness saves from death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that treasure gained by wickedness brings no real benefit.
judaism.tie_back: Wealth gained without righteousness is worthless, which is why the Kural says to let it go.
judaism.source: Proverbs 10:2 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on rejecting wrongly gained wealth; Proverbs stresses righteousness where the Kural stresses compassion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Discerning clearly, a clever person knows both kinds of happiness: the other kind is not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of blamelessness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ranks the happiness of owning and using wealth far below the happiness of a blameless life.
buddhism.tie_back: Wealth that costs one’s blamelessness is not worth keeping, which is the Kural’s point in letting it roll away.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on ranking blamelessness above wealth; the sutta does not name compassion specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for if a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue, as often happens when gain deceives men’s sense and dishonour tramples down honour, the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that wealth taken by force or deceit is soon lost and brings the gods’ punishment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod, like Valluvar, tells us to refuse wealth gained without justice or kindness.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 320-326 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match; Hesiod warns of divine punishment, the Kural simply says to reject such wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There are two sorts of wealth-getting, as I have said; one is a part of household management, the other is retail trade: the former necessary and honorable, while that which consists in exchange is justly censured; for it is unnatural, and a mode by which men gain from one another.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle separates honourable wealth-getting that serves the household from money-making that profits at other people’s expense.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, rejects gain made at the cost of others.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I, Part X (trans. B. Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified wording (the source text runs ‘apart of’, corrected here); Aristotle’s standard is natural versus unnatural gain, not compassion.

kurals.tamil:
உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும்தன் ஒன்னார்த்
தெறுபொருளும் வேந்தன் பொருள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uruporulum ulgu porulumthan onnaarth
theruporulum vendhan porul.
kurals.meaning: Wealth that comes to the crown without an owner, revenue from customs and tolls, and tribute taken from defeated enemies: these are the king’s wealth.
kurals.elementary: Think of a school fund. It gets money from lost-and-found items nobody claims, from small fees for using the playground, and from the prize when the school wins a match against another school. Valluvar lists the kinds of money that belong to a king’s treasury in a similar way.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s one technical verse, listing three lawful sources of royal revenue. Uruporul is ‘wealth that comes of itself’, which Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah explain as ownerless property such as heirless estates and treasure trove, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it as ordinary tax (இறை, வரி). Ulgu porul is customs or toll revenue on goods, and theru porul is tribute or spoil taken from subdued enemies (onnaar). The verse spells out what 755 means in practice: a king’s legitimate income has clear, lawful channels. The sandhi-joined text reads உறுபொருளு முல்கு பொருளுந்தன் னொன்னார்த், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti directs that property whose owner has disappeared be held by the king in trust for three years, after which the king may take it, and elsewhere it sets out duties on merchandise and the king’s share of produce.
hinduism.explanation: The dharma texts set out ownerless property and customs duties as lawful royal income.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu covers two of the Kural’s three categories, unclaimed wealth and customs, almost term for term.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of known passages; verse numbers may vary slightly between editions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Christians in Rome to pay the government its taxes and customs as rightful dues.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s tribute and custom line up closely with the Kural’s tribute and ulgu (customs) as lawful royal revenue.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on customs and tribute as rightful dues, spoken from the payer’s side rather than the king’s.

islam.quote_or_event: “And know that anything you obtain of war booty - then indeed, for Allah is one fifth of it and for the Messenger and for [his] near relatives and the orphans, the needy, and the [stranded] traveler.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an assigns one fifth of the spoils of war to God and the Messenger, to be used for relatives, orphans, the needy and travellers.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s third category, wealth taken from enemies, as a lawful share of public revenue.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches one of the three categories; the Qur’an directs the share to welfare, not simply to the ruler.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Israel asks for a king, Samuel warns that the king will take a tenth of their grain, vineyards and flocks, and will take their fields and servants for his own use.
judaism.explanation: Samuel describes royal revenue as a burden the people will bring on themselves by demanding a king.
judaism.tie_back: Samuel describes the same royal revenue the Kural lists, but warns against its excess.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Samuel’s tone is critical of royal taxation, while the Kural treats it as legitimate.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, the Buddha tells of a wise chaplain who advises a king not to raise taxes to fund a sacrifice, but to give seed, capital and wages to farmers, traders and officials, so that the realm grows prosperous and the treasury fills.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta teaches that a ruler’s revenue should grow out of a thriving people, not from heavier taxes.
buddhism.tie_back: It gives a Buddhist view of the royal treasury the Kural lists, with the stress on lawful and non-oppressive revenue.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the sutta is about economic policy rather than naming the Kural’s three revenue sources.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Iliad opens with Achilles and Agamemnon quarrelling over the division of spoils taken from conquered towns, each claiming his share of the prizes as a right of honour.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, wealth taken from defeated enemies was a recognised part of a king’s possessions and status.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shows the Kural’s theru porul, wealth from subdued foes, as royal income in the heroic world.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Matches only the spoils category, and Homer’s interest is honour and conflict, not public finance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book V of The Wealth of Nations, Adam Smith examines the sources of the sovereign’s revenue, discussing income from crown property and from taxes on land, goods and consumption, including customs duties.
philosophy.explanation: Smith analyses where a state’s income should come from and how to raise it fairly.
philosophy.tie_back: Smith gives a modern, systematic version of the Kural’s short list of lawful royal income.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2
philosophy._accuracy_note: Summary of the chapter’s scope; Smith does not treat spoils of war as revenue.

kurals.tamil:
அருளென்னும் அன்பீன் குழவி பொருளென்னும்
செல்வச் செவிலியால் உண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Arulennum anbeen kuzhavi porulennum
selvach cheviliyaal undu.
kurals.meaning: Compassion is the child that love gives birth to, and it is raised by the rich foster-mother called wealth.
kurals.elementary: Picture a baby born to a loving mother, cared for by a kind nanny who has plenty of food and warm blankets. Valluvar says kindness is like that baby: love gives birth to it, and money helps it grow, because it is easier to help others when you have something to give.
kurals.university: This is one of the Kural’s finest extended metaphors. Arul (compassion for all beings) is the kuzhavi, the infant, born of anbu (love for one’s own; anbeen is anbu plus eenra, ‘borne by love’), and porul is the selvach cheviliyal, the rich wet-nurse or foster-mother (cevili) who raises it. The genealogy reverses the usual worry that wealth corrupts: love begets compassion, but compassion cannot grow into practical kindness without means. It links back to chapter 8, Anbudaimai, which says love begets affection and friendship, and it answers 755 by showing the right relation of wealth to arul and anbu. The sandhi-joined text reads அருளென்னு மன்பீன் குழவி பொருளென்னுஞ், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad’s parting counsel to graduating students tells them to give with faith, to give in plenty, to give with modesty, with awe, and with sympathy.
hinduism.explanation: The teacher links generous giving to an attitude of reverence and fellow-feeling.
hinduism.tie_back: Giving ‘in plenty’ joined to sympathy echoes the Kural’s picture of wealth nursing compassion.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the Upanishad pairs giving with right feeling, but it has no nurse-and-child metaphor.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?”
christianity.explanation: John says that love is real only when a person who has means opens both heart and purse to someone in need.
christianity.tie_back: John links love, compassion and ‘this world’s good’ in the same chain as the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on the love-compassion-means chain; John states it as a test, not a metaphor of nursing.

islam.quote_or_event: “[True] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah... and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask [for help], and for freeing slaves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an defines true righteousness as faith shown in the giving of wealth to those in need, even though one loves that wealth.
islam.tie_back: In both texts, compassion takes practical form through wealth given away.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on wealth as the vehicle of compassion; ‘love’ in the verse is love of the wealth itself, which is a different sense from the Kural’s anbu.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where there is no bread, there is no Torah; where there is no Torah, there is no bread.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah teaches that spiritual life and material sustenance depend on each other.
judaism.tie_back: As the Kural’s compassion needs a well-provided nurse, Torah needs bread in order to flourish.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel of the spiritual depending on the material; the Mishnah speaks of Torah rather than compassion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And they’d hold on to friends by dividing their wealth in four.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the young householder Sigalaka that a wise person keeps friendships alive by managing wealth well and sharing it.
buddhism.tie_back: Here too, well-kept wealth nourishes bonds of love and care.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Moderate match; friendship rather than compassion is the virtue nourished.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Athens set up Kephisodotos’ statue of Eirene (Peace) holding the infant Ploutos (Wealth) in her arms, and Pausanias describes a similar statue at Thebes of Tyche carrying the child Ploutos.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek art pictured wealth as a baby nursed and carried by a goddess.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greek image uses the same nurse-and-infant figure as the Kural, but reversed: in Athens Peace nurses Wealth, while in the Kural Wealth nurses Compassion.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Striking shared metaphor with inverted roles; summarised from memory of Pausanias.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle defines liberality as the virtue of giving to the right people, in the right amounts, at the right time, and notes that the liberal person must also take from the right sources so as to have something to give.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, generosity is a real virtue, but it needs property to work with.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, sees kindness in action as needing wealth to grow.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book IV, Chapter 1
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory; Aristotle’s liberality is narrower than arul.

kurals.tamil:
குன்றேறி யானைப்போர் கண்டற்றால் தன்கைத்தொன்று
உண்டாகச் செய்வான் வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kundreri yaanaippor kandatraal thankaiththondru
undaagach cheyvaan vinai.
kurals.meaning: Someone who starts a venture with money already in hand is like a person watching an elephant fight from a hilltop, safe and able to see everything.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two huge elephants pushing and fighting in a field. If you stood in the middle, you could get hurt. But if you climb a hill and watch from the top, you are safe and can see everything. Valluvar says that starting a big job with savings in your pocket is like watching from that hill.
kurals.university: The simile draws on a familiar sight in Sangam India, the royal elephant fight, which was deadly to anyone on the ground and a pleasure to watch from high up. Thankaiththu ondru undaaga means ‘with something being in one’s own hand’, that is, having one’s own funds, and cheyvaan vinai is ‘the work of one who acts’. Parimelazhagar explains that such a person has no need to depend on others and so can watch the struggle of the undertaking without fear, while Kalaignar adds the image of not being caught between the fighting elephants. The sandhi-joined text reads கண்டற்றாற் றன்கைத்தொன் றுண்டாகச், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Wealth brings about accessions of wealth, like elephants capturing (wild) elephants.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna compares money that brings in more money to trained elephants used to capture wild ones.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts use the elephant to show that someone who starts with wealth in hand is in a position of strength.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section VIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shared elephant imagery and shared idea of capital’s advantage, though the images make different points.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the builder who checks his funds before starting as an image of counting the cost of discipleship.
christianity.tie_back: The builder with enough in hand is the Kural’s watcher on the hill, while the one without is caught and mocked.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close practical parallel; Jesus uses it as a figure for discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one’s own hands. The Prophet of Allah, David used to eat from the earnings of his manual labor.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises living from one’s own earnings rather than depending on others.
islam.tie_back: The hadith’s pride in self-earned means matches the Kural’s trust in having one’s own wealth in hand.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the value of self-reliance; the hadith is about the dignity of labour, not the safety of capital.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Rabbi Yitzḥak says: A person should always divide his money into three; he should bury one-third in the ground, and invest one-third in business, and keep one-third in his possession.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud advises keeping part of one’s wealth liquid and at hand, so that one is never left without resources.
judaism.tie_back: Rabbi Yitzhak’s third kept in hand is exactly the Kural’s wealth ‘in one’s own hand’ that makes a venture safe.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 42a (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on keeping money at hand; the bracketed explanations of the Koren translation are omitted.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One portion is to enjoy. Two parts invest in work. And the fourth should be kept for times of trouble.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha advises the householder to invest half his wealth in work and keep a quarter in reserve for hard times.
buddhism.tie_back: Working with capital and a reserve is the secure position the Kural pictures as the hilltop.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close practical match on working from one’s own funds with a reserve.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But let it be your care to order your work properly, that in the right season your barns may be full of victual.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells Perses to plan his work so that his stores are full when they are needed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Full barns before the season turns are the Kural’s funds in hand before a venture begins.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate match on having resources ready in advance; there is no image of safe watching.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle tells how Thales, mocked for his poverty, foresaw a large olive harvest, used a small sum to reserve all the olive presses in Miletus and Chios in advance, and made a fortune when the harvest came.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle uses the story to show that a philosopher can make money easily when he chooses to, by having funds ready at the right moment.
philosophy.tie_back: Thales with deposits in hand, waiting calmly for the harvest, is the Kural’s watcher on the hill.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I, Part XI (trans. B. Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known anecdote in the same chapter; the point is foresight more than safety.

kurals.tamil:
செய்க பொருளைச் செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்
எஃகதனிற் கூரிய தில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyga porulaich cherunar serukkarukkum
eqkadhanir kooriya thil.
kurals.meaning: Build up wealth: there is no steel sharper than it for cutting down the pride of your enemies.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a bully who brags that nobody can stand up to him. Then the whole class saves up to build a strong new fence and hire a coach, and suddenly the bully stops bragging. Valluvar says a well-stocked treasury is the sharpest sword against a proud enemy.
kurals.university: The verse opens with a blunt imperative, seyga porulai, ‘make wealth!’, which is rare in the Kural and gives the command its force. Cherunar are foes, serukku is their arrogance, and aRukkum (‘that cuts off’) sets up the image of eqku (எஃகு), steel or a sword, of which nothing is sharper (kooriyadhu il). Parimelazhagar explains that wealth lets a king raise and keep armies and allies, and so humbles enemies without his having to strike himself. Solomon Pappaiah addresses the verse to anyone who wants to achieve something. The sandhi-joined text reads செருக்கறுக்கு மெஃகதனிற், which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra holds that the army is rooted in the treasury (koshamulo hi dandah), so a king with a full treasury can raise and keep the force needed to subdue enemies.
hinduism.explanation: Indian statecraft ranked the treasury as the source of military power.
hinduism.tie_back: For Kautilya as for Valluvar, wealth is the real weapon behind every other weapon.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VIII (on the elements of sovereignty), trans. R. Shamasastry
hinduism._accuracy_note: Well-known maxim summarised from memory; book and chapter reference is approximate.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For wisdom is a defence, and money is a defence: but the excellency of knowledge is, that wisdom giveth life to them that have it.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher places money beside wisdom as a protection, while ranking wisdom higher.
christianity.tie_back: Money as a defence is the protective side of the Kural’s sharp steel.
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial match: the verse speaks of defence rather than attack, and it ranks wisdom above money.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy... And whatever you spend in the cause of Allah will be fully repaid to you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the community to prepare strength to deter enemies and promises that spending for this cause will be repaid.
islam.tie_back: In the verse, spending builds the strength that humbles an enemy, much as the Kural’s wealth cuts down a foe’s pride.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on wealth spent to deter enemies; the verse’s focus is preparedness rather than wealth itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For to be in the shelter of wisdom is to be also in the shelter of money, and the advantage of intelligence is that wisdom preserves the life of the one who possesses it.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet says money, like wisdom, gives shelter from life’s threats.
judaism.tie_back: Kohelet’s shelter of money is the defensive side of the Kural’s weapon against enemies.
judaism.source: Ecclesiastes 7:12 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Partial match: shelter and protection, not an offensive weapon.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, the Buddha tells how a king who failed to give wealth to the poor set off a slide into theft, weapons and violence, showing that neglecting material provision breeds conflict.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta traces social violence back to poverty the ruler failed to relieve.
buddhism.tie_back: Seen from the opposite side, wealth rightly used is what keeps hostility from arising, which is a gentler version of the Kural’s weapon.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Loose match: Buddhism does not praise wealth as a weapon, so this is the nearest related teaching.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Thucydides, the Spartan king Archidamus warns his people before the Peloponnesian War that war is a matter less of arms than of money, which is what makes arms useful.
greek_mythology.explanation: Archidamus argues that Athens’ wealth makes it more dangerous than Sparta’s soldiers alone can handle.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Archidamus and Valluvar agree that wealth is the sharpest weapon in a conflict.
greek_mythology.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 1.83
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match, paraphrased from memory; this is Greek history rather than myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero, urging war against Mark Antony, calls unlimited money the sinews of war (nervos belli, pecuniam infinitam), a phrase that became proverbial.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that money is what holds a war effort together.
philosophy.tie_back: The sinews of war and the sharpest steel are the same idea: wealth is what defeats an enemy.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Well-known phrase, not checked against a live text; Cicero is an orator-philosopher speaking in a political setting.

kurals.tamil:
ஒண்பொருள் காழ்ப்ப இயற்றியார்க்கு எண்பொருள்
ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Onporul kaazhppa iyatriyaarkku enporul
enai irandum orungu.
kurals.meaning: For those who have built up an abundance of good, honestly earned wealth, the other two aims of life, virtue and happiness, come together easily.
kurals.elementary: Think of a garden. Once the soil is rich and well watered, flowers and vegetables both grow easily. Valluvar says honest wealth is like that rich soil: once you have it, goodness and happiness grow easily too.
kurals.university: The closing verse ties the chapter to the three aims of life (muppaal: aram, porul, inbam) that give the Kural its three books. Onporul is ‘bright’ or excellent wealth, which the commentators take to mean wealth gained by good means, echoing 754; kaazhppa (from kaazh, hard core) means firmly and abundantly; enporul is ‘an easy thing’ (en, easy); and enai irandum orungu means ‘the other two, together’. Parimelazhagar explains that for such a person virtue and pleasure are both easily attained, and Kalaignar names the three purusharthas explicitly. The verse repeats the pairing in 754 and closes the chapter’s argument that honestly earned wealth underpins a complete life. The sandhi-joined text reads இயற்றியார்க் கெண்பொரு ளேனை யிரண்டு மொருங்கு, which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Kautilya holds that wealth and wealth alone is important, inasmuch as charity and desire depend upon wealth for their realisation.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya argues that among the three aims of life, artha comes first, because dharma and kama both depend on it.
hinduism.tie_back: Kautilya and Valluvar make the same argument: once wealth is secured, the other two aims follow.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book I, Chapter 7 (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on artha as the root of dharma and kama; Valluvar adds that the wealth must be honestly earned.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to teach the rich to enjoy God’s gifts and use their wealth for good works.
christianity.tie_back: Paul pairs enjoyment (‘all things to enjoy’) with good works, the same two ends the Kural says wealth makes easy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on enjoyment and virtue flowing from wealth, but Paul warns against trusting riches.

islam.quote_or_event: “But seek, through that which Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and [yet], do not forget your share of the world. And do good as Allah has done good to you.”
islam.explanation: Qarun’s people advise him to use his wealth to seek the hereafter and do good, without neglecting his rightful share of worldly enjoyment.
islam.tie_back: The verse joins virtue and lawful enjoyment through wealth, which is the Kural’s ‘other two, together’.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match; the verse is a warning to the arrogant Qarun, who ignored it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Remember that it is the ETERNAL your God who gives you the power to get wealth, in fulfillment of the covenant made on oath with your fathers, as is still the case.”
judaism.explanation: Moses reminds Israel that the ability to prosper comes from God and serves the covenant.
judaism.tie_back: Wealth is placed inside a larger moral purpose, as the Kural places porul in the service of aram and inbam.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 8:18 (JPS Tanakh, Revised JPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Partial match: it frames wealth as serving a higher end but does not name virtue and pleasure as its fruits.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “I’ve achieved the goal for which an astute layperson wishes to gain wealth. I don’t regret what I’ve done.”
buddhism.explanation: The householder who has used legitimate wealth to support family, guard against loss, make offerings and give to the virtuous can look back without regret.
buddhism.tie_back: His fulfilled goal, joining enjoyment with merit, is the Kural’s aram and inbam gained through porul.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.61, Pattakamma Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match; the sutta’s full verse lists both enjoyment and merit as the fruits of legitimate wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas, granted his wish that everything he touched would turn to gold, found that his food and drink also turned to gold, and he begged Dionysus to take the gift back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas learns that wealth pursued for its own sake destroys the very pleasures it was meant to buy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Midas is the reverse of the Kural: wealth cut off from virtue gives neither happiness nor goodness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Contrast story; the version in which Midas turns his daughter to gold is a later retelling (Hawthorne), not Ovid.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle says that happiness also needs external goods, since it is impossible, or not easy, to do noble acts without the proper equipment, and many actions are performed through friends, riches and political power as instruments.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that a complete happy life needs enough external resources to act on one’s virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s riches as the instruments of noble action and happiness state the same idea as Valluvar’s wealth that makes virtue and pleasure easy.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, Chapter 8
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match; paraphrase of a well-known passage in Ross’s translation, not checked verbatim.
